casos.pregunta: ¿Qué diferencia hay entre una transacción y un bloqueo optimista en una base de datos relacional, y cuándo usarías cada uno?
casos.respuesta: Una transacción agrupa operaciones para que se cumplan todas o ninguna, y la base mantiene aislamiento mediante bloqueos mientras dura. El bloqueo optimista no bloquea: cada fila lleva una versión y, al guardar, se comprueba que no haya cambiado; si cambió, se rechaza y se reintenta. Usaría transacciones con bloqueo pesimista cuando hay mucha contención sobre la misma fila, y optimista cuando los conflictos son raros y quiero no retener conexiones.

casos.pregunta: What is the difference between a database transaction and optimistic locking, and when would you use each one?
casos.respuesta: A transaction groups operations so that all of them happen or none does, and the database keeps isolation with locks while it runs. Optimistic locking does not lock: each row carries a version and on save we check it did not change; if it did, the write is rejected and retried. I would use pessimistic locking when there is heavy contention on the same row, and optimistic when conflicts are rare and I do not want to hold connections.

casos.pregunta: Design, at a high level, a service that sends emails asynchronously without losing messages if the server restarts.
casos.respuesta: I would use a persistent message queue, for example RabbitMQ with durable queues. The service stores the send request in an outbox table inside the same transaction as the business change and a process publishes it to the queue, so nothing is lost if the server restarts. The consumer acknowledges the message only after sending the email and, on failure, retries with growing waits and then moves it to a dead-letter queue. Each send carries an identifier so a retry does not send the email twice.
